name: First screen duel
goal: More first-time visitors run a check on a sample pull request from the first screen they land on.
product: Experiment Guard checks every pull request against the A/B tests currently running in Flagsmith, and blocks the ones that would silently corrupt a running test: a renamed event, a removed exposure call, a changed visitor ID and so on. This web app is its dashboard. It has a playground where anyone can run the guard on sample pull requests and see the verdict.
today: A dashboard overview titled "Pull requests": four tiles of counts (checks, blocked, clean pass rate, median check time), charts of block rate and override rate, a list of guarded experiments and a list of the latest checks. Nothing on it says what the product is for. To run a check, a visitor has to notice a small "Run all scenarios" button in the page header, or open "Playground" in the navigation and press Run there.
visitors: People who followed a link from the project's README or from a post about feature flags and A/B testing. Mostly software engineers; also product managers, data analysts and engineering managers. Most give a new tool under a minute. Many could not say what an exposure event or a sample ratio mismatch is. Some distrust anything that can block their pull requests. They arrive on a laptop, with no account and nothing installed.

statements: Experiment Guard checks a pull request against the experiments that are running in Flagsmith right now.
It blocks changes that would corrupt a running experiment's data, such as renaming a tracked event, removing the exposure call or changing the visitor ID.
The playground has 22 sample pull requests. The guard blocks 7 of them, warns about 4 and lets the other 11 through.
Running a check here takes a few seconds and needs no account, no install and no Flagsmith project.
A check only reads from Flagsmith. It changes nothing there.
It runs as a GitHub Action, a command-line tool and an MCP server for coding agents.
